Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:7: And anyone who is able to study Torah and does not study it, of him Scripture says (Jeremiah 2:5), "thus says the LORD: what wrong did your fathers find in Me, that they distanced themselves from Me and went after vanity and became vain?"
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:8: One who washes his shoes and goes out to the marketplace is among the haughty of spirit. One whose chin points to the side, whose hat is tilted backward, whose sandal is over its fellow, or whose tefillin straps are in his hand and he swings them while walking in the marketplace, is among the haughty of spirit. And all the haughty of spirit resemble idolatry, as it is said (Deuteronomy 7:26), "and you shall not bring an abomination into your house," and elsewhere it says (Proverbs 16:5), "every proud heart is an abomination to the LORD" - "abomination" is said here and "abomination" is said there: just as the "abomination" said here is idolatry, so the "abomination" said there is idolatry. It is said elsewhere (Deuteronomy 13:14), "worthless men have gone out," and it is said elsewhere (II Samuel 23:6), "and the worthless are all like thorns thrust away" - but whoever walks in His ways is blessed, as it is said (Psalms 103:20), "bless the LORD, His angels, mighty in strength, who do His word" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:9: Further, to complete the acquisition of the attribute of humility, one must distance himself from envy, desire, and honor, which remove a person from this world and the World to Come (chapter 4:26) - and the pious Rabbi Yosef Yavetz, peace be upon him, elaborated on this - and especially envy is a branch of anger.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:10: And it is written in Sefer Beit Middot, found among us in manuscript, several things about the disgrace of the attribute of envy (Gate of Envy) - I have seen fit to copy his words, since they are relevant to practice - these are its words: the attribute of envy is a branch of anger, and no person escapes it, for we see that all people are drawn after one another - for when a person sees that his fellow has acquired some worldly matter, whether kinds of food, or clothing, or building a house, or gathering wealth, then he toils to attain the same, for he thinks, my fellow has this, I too shall have such - and King Solomon, peace be upon him, hinted at this matter, saying (Ecclesiastes 4:4), "I have seen that all labor and all skill in work come from one man's envy of another."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:11: And whoever is overcome by this attribute is disgraceful, for this envy shall bring him to covetousness - for when a person does not take to heart and envy what is in his own possession, then he covets, and the Torah said (Exodus 20:14), "you shall not covet." And when he covets, then he steals, as it is written (Micah 2:2), "and they covet fields and steal them." And a person overcome by covetousness is close to transgressing the Ten Commandments - for there was a story of a certain man who had a wicked neighbor, with a wall separating between them - and the wicked one coveted his wife and some of his possessions. One day, on Sabbath eve, he heard the man say to his wife, I wish to leave today on a business trip - and so he did. What did that wicked man do? He went on Sabbath night and broke down the wall separating between them, transgressing "remember the Sabbath day to keep it holy." He went and raped the woman he coveted and lay with her, transgressing "you shall not commit adultery." Afterward he began to rob the money - the woman cried out, and he stood over her and killed her, transgressing "you shall not murder." And when he stole and robbed what he coveted, he transgressed "you shall not steal" and "you shall not covet." The next day his father and mother came and rebuked him - he rose and struck them, transgressing "honor your father and your mother." And afterward he was brought before the court and testified together with his worthless fellow that those objects he took were his own pledge, held in pledge from the woman's husband, transgressing "you shall not bear [false witness]." In the end the matter was revealed and publicized, and his evil became known, and out of shame he went to evil ways and denied the living God, transgressing "I am [the LORD your God]" - and in the end he became devoted to idolatry, transgressing "you shall have no [other gods]," "you shall not bow to them," and "nor serve them" - and all this was caused by the aspect of covetousness. It follows that one who covets is close to transgressing the entire Torah.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:12: But there is another way, close to it, to discern how envy and covetousness corrupt a person - and of this King Solomon, peace be upon him, said (Proverbs 23:17), "let your heart not envy sinners, but rather the fear of the LORD all day." When a person envies sinners and sees their wealth and success, and sees the righteous disparaged and disciplined with sufferings, through this his soul becomes disgusted with God's judgments and statutes, and he shall reject those who learn and fulfill Torah, along the lines of what is said in Malachi (3:13-15), "your words have been harsh against Me," and so on, "you have said, it is vain to serve God, and what profit is it that we have kept His charge, and that we have walked in mourning before the LORD of Hosts? And now we call the arrogant happy; indeed those who work wickedness are built up; indeed they test God, and escape." And this matter brings folly into people's minds and turns their hearts backward, when they see a wicked person doing well and a righteous person doing badly - and through this they go in the stubbornness of their hearts and say, so-and-so did such-and-such and he is rich and successful, so let us also do the same, and what happened to him shall also happen to us - and all this comes from the aspect of envy, envying the wicked and coveting their wealth and tranquility, and therefore casting off from themselves the yoke of the commandments.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:13: But the righteous do not envy the wicked and do not covet either their wealth or their tranquility, for they think that their wealth is stored up for their own harm, and their tranquility is to destroy them, from the abundance of good treasured for the righteous - and he shall think that the poverty and distress of the righteous are to refine and purify them and increase their level for the World to Come - and there is no doubt that whoever thinks this way shall not covet or envy, but rather rejoice when he sees the tranquility of the wicked, and say, if it is so for those who provoke Him, how much more so for those who do His will, that He shall give and give again.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:14: Envy comes from a defect of the soul - if he envies a person's beauty, or his might, or his wealth, it follows that he is not content with what the Name, blessed be He, decreed upon him - and this resembles a servant who has a complaint against his master's deed and is not satisfied with his affairs - such a servant is not faithful. All the more so it is not fitting to complain against the Creator, blessed be He, all of whose deeds are upright and wise, that one should not question Him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:15: And whoever envies shall come to strife, as you find with Korach, who envied the honor of Elitzafan ben Uzziel, and through this he and his nursing children and their faction were destroyed from the world.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:16: Envy is like an illness of the body for people, and brings on consumption. The sage said to his son, beware of envy, for it is recognized in you, since your face changes because of the evil of your heart - and that person you envy rejoices at the sorrow of your heart - so why should you make your enemies rejoice, that they take vengeance and rejoice at you?
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:17: The envious person robs his own soul, for he mourns constantly, and his intellect is diminished by the abundance of envy hidden within him, and his heart has no leisure to study, to pray with intent, and to perform good deeds - and every person finds a sweet taste except the envious one, for he does not taste a sweet taste in his food until his fellow's good fortune is reversed.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:18: And every hatred has hope of resolution - for if he hates his fellow who robbed him, once the robbery is returned to him he shall remove the hatred from his heart, and likewise every hatred that depends on a matter, once that matter is repaired for you, the hatred shall be nullified from his heart - except for one who hates his fellow out of envy. And the sage said, do not envy your fellow for what he has, for he shall enjoy it while you shall be filled with worry, grief, distress, and trouble - and the sage said, the covetous and the envious were created only for anger.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:19: The sages of Israel pray, "may our envy not be upon others, nor others' envy upon us" (Yerushalmi Berachot, chapter 4, halachah 2). And why did they pray concerning others regarding this attribute more than the other attributes? Rather, the matter is this: how many people cause others to envy them when they wear fine clothing that shall cause envy - and therefore they would pray, lest they cause envy to others in this way - and the Torah says (Leviticus 19:14), "and you shall not place a stumbling block before the blind." Therefore it is a good measure for a person not to wear excessively fine and impressive clothing, neither he, his wife, nor the people of his household, and likewise in the matter of foods and other matters, so that others not envy him. Also, whoever the Holy One, blessed be He, has bestowed wealth and possessions upon should be yielding toward the rich and the poor, and conduct himself with them calmly and do kindness with them - and we have already elaborated on the matter of how to be beloved by every person; then they shall not envy him nor covet what is his - but it is fitting for a person to rise to good levels that are an ornament to him, that others envy him and covet to make themselves like him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:20: And whoever is careful not to envy, his body does not decay and the worm does not rule over him, as it is written (Proverbs 14:30), "and envy is the rot of the bones" - meaning, whoever has envy, his bones rot. And so a person should distance himself from envy and covetousness, and not covet anything that is in others' possession - and he should not say, I shall covet something of my fellow's affairs and give him money for that matter, if he intends to sell - for then it is forbidden for this one to pressure him, since he shall be ashamed to turn him away empty-handed, and it follows that this is coercion. And all the more so if the one who covets is distinguished - for if he asks some request, they shall not refuse him to his face - it is forbidden for him to ask for what is in his possession, or to take it to show that he desires it, and he should not demand that thing unless he knows that his fellow shall give it to him with a willing soul.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:21: A parable of the covetous man and the envious man: they were walking together on the road, and a king met them. The king said to them, one of you shall ask something of me, and it shall be given to him, and his fellow shall receive double - and the covetous man desired the double portion, while the envious man did not wish to ask, since he would be envious if his fellow received double. In the end the covetous man pressed the envious man to ask first - so the envious man asked that one of his own eyes be gouged out, and his fellow's two.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:22: See how many evils depend on envy - for the primordial serpent envied Adam and caused death to come to the world, and of him a curse is said (Genesis 3:14), "upon your belly you shall go, and dust you shall eat." See what happened to Cain, to Korach, to Balaam, to Achitophel, to Gehazi, to Adoniyahu, to Absalom, and to Uzziah, who set their eyes on what was not fitting for them - and not only was what they sought not given to them, but even what was already in their possession was taken from them. From all these a person shall learn and be careful of envy and covetousness, and think that even what is in his own possession is not truly his, for tomorrow it comes and is gone, and what benefit is it to him that it is not truly his - and of this it is said (Proverbs 27:1), "for you do not know what a day may bring forth."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:23: A great reward is there for a person careful of envy and covetousness - for most transgressions, if a person transgresses them and is ashamed, he refrains from them because of the shame; it follows that the reward for this comes because he restrains himself from envy and covetousness. For one who refrains from robbery and theft is afraid lest it become known and revealed and he be caught and shamed and suffer great loss.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:24: But envy and covetousness are hidden in the heart, concealed from people's eyes, so that no one can discern in him whether he is covetous or envious, since this matter is entrusted to the heart - and if he restrains himself from them, of him Scripture says (Leviticus 19:14), "and you shall fear your God."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:25: And although envy is very bad, there is a context in which it is very good, and it is one of the attributes of the supernal beings - when he directs his envy toward the fear of the Name, as it is said (ibid. 23:17), "let your heart not envy sinners, but rather the fear of the LORD all day" - and of this the Sages said (Bava Batra 21a), the envy of scholars increases wisdom - if a person sees another studying, envy shall take hold in his heart and he shall say, this one studies all day, I too shall do so - and likewise with all the other mitzvot and good attributes, each shall envy his fellow and take hold of his fellow's good deeds. And if he sees a wicked person who has two or three good attributes, through this they shall envy him and do them too.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:26: But one who envies his fellow who is occupied with Torah, mitzvot, and good deeds, and does not envy him in a way that he thinks, this one does good deeds, I too shall do so - but rather thinks in his heart and envies him because he has more merits than himself, and devises stratagems to nullify him and confuse him from his Torah and good deeds - this envy is a bad illness, sinning and causing others to sin, and he is a partner of Jeroboam son of Nevat.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:27: And a person should always honor those who fear Heaven, those who study Torah, and those who fulfill mitzvot, and give them a hand, and assist them with his own body, his money, and all his ability - and then others shall envy him and think, we too shall do so, and they shall also honor and help us - and through [doing it] not for its own sake, one comes to [do it] for its own sake.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:28: And were it not for envy, the world would not endure - for then no one would plant a vineyard, no one would marry a wife, and no one would build a house, since all these matters come about because one person envies another. One who builds a house shall take it to heart to do so [seeing his neighbor's house], and likewise regarding a wife, each shall envy his fellow.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:29: And since the world depends on envy, one should direct all envy toward the sake of Heaven - if he builds a house, let him build within it a room to study Torah in, and let his house be a meeting house for the wise, and to bring in guests and do kindnesses for people - for had Abraham not envied, he would not have acquired heaven and earth. And when did he envy? When he asked Melchizedek, how did you leave the ark? He said to him, through the charity we performed there. He said to him, and what did you have in the ark to do charity with - were there poor people there? Were there not only Noah and his sons there, and with whom did you do charity? He said to him, with the animals, beasts, and birds, for we did not sleep, but gave them their food before them. At that moment Abraham said to him, had you not done charity with the animals, beasts, and birds, you would not have left the ark - and if I do charity with people, created in the image of God, all the more so! At that moment, "and he planted an eshel [tamarisk] in Beersheba" - the acrostic for eating, drinking, and escorting. And of this a person should increase his envy.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:30: And also a person should envy sinners and the wicked, to fight against them and rebuke them, as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Sanhedrin 81b), whoever has relations with an Aramean woman [publicly], the zealous confront him. Moses envied [was zealous against] the Egyptian, as it is said (Exodus 2:12), "and he struck the Egyptian." And we also find Elijah (I Kings 19:10), "I have been very zealous for the LORD, the God of Hosts, for the children of Israel have forsaken Your covenant." And so it is said of Pinchas (Numbers 25:11), "in his being zealous with My zeal among them" - and the Name gave him his reward for this, as it is said, "therefore say, behold, I give him My covenant of peace" - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:31: Further, to complete the attribute of humility, a person must conduct himself with the conditions Torah scholars conduct themselves with, as Rambam, peace be upon him, wrote in chapter 5 of Hilchot De'ot.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:32: And concerning the conditions of a Torah scholar, they explained in Tractate Berachot (43b) - these are their own words: our Rabbis taught, six things are disgraceful for a Torah scholar: he should not go out to the marketplace perfumed; he should not go out alone at night; he should not go out with patched shoes; he should not converse with a woman in the marketplace; he should not recline at a gathering of the ignorant; and he should not be the last to enter the study hall. And some say, he should not take large strides, and should not walk with an upright, erect stature - to this point their own words. And for each of these they explained a reason there in the Gemara, and we shall not copy all its words so as not to be lengthy.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:33: And what is more relevant to the matter of pride is "he should not walk with an upright, erect stature" - and they explained there: Rabbi Yehudah said, whoever walks with an upright, erect stature, even four cubits, is as though he pushes against the feet of the Shechinah, as it is written (Isaiah 6:3), "the whole earth is full of His glory" - to this point. And the reason is that he is proud and shows that he has no master ruling over him, for it is the way of a servant to walk with humility and a bowed head before his master. And all his other matters, in his dress and his speech, he shall conduct with the conditions Rambam, peace be upon him, explained there - and he shall certainly be perfected in the attribute of humility, in its general and its particular aspects.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:34: And when a person strives in the attribute of humility, in all its details written in this Gate, he shall find that included in the acquisition of the attribute of humility is the acquisition of all good attributes, and included in the attribute of pride is the sum of all disgraceful attributes - and this is along the lines of "there is nothing higher than ONEG [delight] and nothing lower than NEGA [affliction]" (see Sefer Yetzirah, chapter 2, mishnah 7) - and it has already been explained that the proud person is struck with afflictions, since one of the reasons afflictions come is haughtiness of spirit, and it is written (Leviticus 14:56), "and for a rising [se'et] and for a scab [sapachat]" - it follows that whoever has no humility lacks the good attributes. And so it is explained in the Baraita of Tractate Kallah (chapter 3), of blessed memory: be like the lower threshold of the house - for this house, if it has no threshold, appears deficient, as though ruined; you too must have humility, and even if you are perfected in all attributes, if you lack humility you are deficient - for so people say, what a great man is so-and-so, were it not for his pride - to teach you this. Rather, "he who fears God shall come forth from them all." Rava said, just as the threshold sets the doors in place for locking and opening, so humility is a fence for wisdom - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:35: Concerning the merit of humility, there are many merits, besides those we explained in chapter 3. Further, they, of blessed memory, said in Sotah (5b): Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said, how great are the lowly of spirit - for when the Temple stood, a person offering a burnt offering had the reward of a burnt offering in his hand, one offering a meal-offering had the reward of a meal-offering in his hand - but whoever has a lowly mind, Scripture considers it as though he had offered all the sacrifices together, and moreover, his prayer is not rejected, as it is said (Psalms 51:19), "a broken and crushed heart, God, You shall not despise." And Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said, whoever sets his own ways [with humility] in this world merits to see the salvation of the Holy One, blessed be He, as it is said (ibid. 50:23), "and to him who sets [sam] his way, I shall show him the salvation of God" - do not read "sam" [sets] but "sham" [there].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:36: And also in the World to Come his merit is great, as they expounded in Megillah (15b), on the verse (Isaiah 28:5), "on that day the LORD of Hosts shall be a crown of glory" - Rabbi Elazar said in the name of Rabbi Chanina, the Holy One, blessed be He, is destined to be a crown on the head of every single righteous person, and so on - and they said, one might think for all - therefore Scripture says, "to the remnant of His people" - to whoever makes himself like the remnant [i.e., humble].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:37: Further, so that you recognize how many merits are in humility, I have seen fit to copy the words of Menorat HaMaor by Rabbi Yisrael, of blessed memory, who elaborated on its merits - these are its words: great is humility, for which Abraham our father, peace be upon him, was praised - because the great men of his generation exalted him and called him "my lord," as it is said (Genesis 23:6), "hear us, my lord" - and he, peace be upon him, would lower himself among them and submit before them, conducting himself with them with the attribute of humility and modesty, even with the lowly, as it is said (ibid. 23:12), "and Abraham bowed down," and so on. And although he was a prophet, a prince, mighty, and wealthy, he was modest and humble and did not consider himself anything, saying (ibid. 18:27), "and I am dust and ashes." Prophet: as it is written (ibid. 20:7), "return the man's wife, for he is a prophet." Prince: as it is written (ibid. 23:6), "you are a prince of God among us." Mighty: as it is written (ibid. 14:15), "and he divided his forces against them by night, he and his servants, and struck them." Wealthy: as it is written (ibid. 13:2), "and Abram was very heavy with livestock," and so on.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:38: Great is humility, for which Isaac our father, peace be upon him, was praised - for Abimelech expelled him from his kingdom, and he prospered in all his deeds and all his ways, as it is said (Genesis 26:12), "and Isaac sowed," and so on - and from the abundance of his wealth the Philistines envied him, as it is said (ibid. 26:14), "and he had possession of flocks," and so on, "and the Philistines envied him," and so on - and when Abimelech came to him, he did not repay him according to his deeds, but out of the abundance of his humility received him with a pleasant countenance and fed and gave drink to him and his men, as it is said (ibid. 26:30), "and he made them a feast," and so on, "and Isaac sent them away," and so on. And this is from the attribute of humility and piety, not to repay the doer of evil according to his evil, but to repay him with good for evil.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:39: Great is humility, for which Jacob our father, peace be upon him, was praised - and because of his humility he would honor Esau his brother, since he came into the air of the world just one moment before him, and his messenger would say to him (Genesis 32:5), "thus says your servant Jacob" - and it was not that he feared him, lest he kill or be killed. Rabbi, when he would write to Antoninus, would say, "the utterance of your servant Judah" - he said, I am no better than my ancestors (Bereishit Rabbah 75:5).
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:40: Great is humility, for which Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, was praised, as it is said (Numbers 12:3), "and the man Moses was very humble" - what does "more than all men" teach? Rather, that he was humble and did not become proud through any of the attributes people are accustomed to becoming proud through, such as kingship, prophecy, and wisdom - and although he had all the good attributes in the world, his heart was not proud through them, not even one of them. When he was in Egypt, although he was like the son of Pharaoh's daughter, he suffered along with Israel and shared in their burden. Even when he had the greatness of Heaven, he did not abandon his humility, as it is said (Exodus 17:12), "and they took a stone and placed it under him, and he sat upon it" - did Moses not have a cushion or a pillow to sit upon? Rather, Moses said, Israel are in distress, I too shall be in distress with them. And even at the time of strife, he did not abandon his humility, as it is said (Numbers 16:25), "and Moses arose and went to Dathan and Aviram" - and he did not become proud, saying, do they dispute against the Holy One, blessed be He, while I am like a king and should go after them [to be summoned]? Rather, in all his matters he was humble. And so you find, when Eldad and Meidad prophesied, what did Joshua say to him? (Numbers 11:28), "my lord Moses, restrain them" - and what did he say to him? Are you envious for my sake, and so on - even if slaves and maidservants become prophets, [I would be glad] - and you seek that I alone be a prophet? I, who requested these seventy elders, as it is said (ibid. 11:14), "I cannot bear it alone" - and moreover, from the start I was fleeing from authority, as it is said (Exodus 4:13), "send, please, by the hand of whomever You will send." And likewise, because of his humility, he did not gaze at the Shechinah at the thornbush, as it is said (Exodus 3:6), "and Moses hid his face" - and he received a reward, as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explained (Berachot 7a), as a reward for "and Moses hid his face," he merited a radiant countenance. Therefore, when the Holy One, blessed be He, praised him, He praised him only with the attribute of humility, as it is said, "and the man Moses was very humble" - "wise," "pious" is not said, but only "humble."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:41: Great is humility, for which Aaron, peace be upon him, was praised - as is the way of the world, that a person honors his own house with worn-out clothes, and so on, as we copied in the Gate of Fear, chapter 15 - and likewise for it Elazar the priest, the Levites, and the sons of Kehat were praised, as we wrote there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:42: Great is humility, through which Samuel the prophet, peace be upon him, became great - for the angel called him three times, and he thought Eli was calling him, and he trembled and awoke from his sleep to come to him three times, as it is said (I Samuel 3:8), "and the LORD called Samuel again, a third time" - and he did not become proud and say, how long will this one keep calling me while I run and come to him - and had he been asleep and not risen, this great prophecy would have been lost to him. And moreover, he would wander from place to place for Israel's needs, but not for his own need, as it is said (I Samuel 7:16), "and he went from year to year." And moreover, when Israel said to him, "give us a king to judge us" (I Samuel 8:6), he did not say to them, behold, I am like a king over you, and yet you seek a king.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:43: Great is humility, through which Saul became great - when Samuel said to him (I Samuel 9:20), "and for whom is all the desire of Israel? Is it not for you?" - he made himself small out of his own humility and said to him (ibid. 9:21), "am I not a Benjamite, of the smallest of the tribes of Israel, and my family the least," and so on. And at the time they sought to anoint him king, he went and hid himself among the baggage until they cast lots, as it is said (I Samuel 10:22), "and the LORD said, behold, he is hidden among the baggage."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:44: Rabbi Yannai says, Scripture spells out thirteen good attributes concerning King Saul, peace be upon him. One: humility - "am I not a Benjamite." Two: that he heard his own disgrace and was silent, as it is said (I Samuel 10:27), "and the worthless sons said, how shall this one save us," and so on, "and he was as one deaf," as one who did not know. Three: that he forgave his own insult, as it is said (I Samuel 11:12), "who is he who said, shall Saul reign over us? Bring the men, that we may put them to death," and it is written, "and Saul said, no man shall be put to death this day." Four: that he was careful with the mitzvah of tzitzit, as it is said (I Samuel 24:4), "and David arose and cut off the corner of Saul's robe secretly" - "corner" is the tzitzit, as it is said (Numbers 15:38), "and they shall put upon the tzitzit of the corner." Five: that he would provide dowries for all the daughters of Israel, giving to whoever had none of her own, as it is said (II Samuel 1:24), "daughters of Israel, weep over Saul, who clothed you in scarlet with luxuries, who put ornaments of gold upon your apparel." Six: that he had the strength to repent - for although Samuel told him, "I will not return with you" (I Samuel 15:26), he would say to him, forgive, please, my sin and return with me, that I may bow to the LORD. Seven: that he was modest, as it is said (I Samuel 24:3), "and he came to the sheepfolds by the road, where there was a cave, and Saul went in to relieve himself" - "sheepfolds" and "a cave" [both mentioned, teaching he covered himself doubly] - and nevertheless he covered himself, and for that modesty he was saved from a strange death, as we learn in Tractate Berachot (62b) - and it is said, "and [he] said [to kill you], but [my eye] spared you" (I Samuel 24:11) - and it said, it should say "I said" and "I spared"! Rabbi Elazar said, David said to Saul, according to the law of the Torah I am permitted to kill you, for you are a pursuer, and whoever comes to kill you, rise early and kill him first - but your own modesty spared you. And what was Saul's modesty? As it is said, "and he came to the sheepfolds by the road," and so on - it is taught, a fold within a fold, and a cave within a cave; "to relieve himself" - Rabbi Elazar said, that he covered himself like a sukkah. Eight: that he squandered his own money but spared the money of Israel, as it is said (I Samuel 11:6-7), "and the spirit of God prospered upon Saul when he heard," and so on, "and he took a pair of oxen and cut them in pieces." Nine: that he ate ordinary food in purity, as it is said (I Samuel 20:26), "and Saul did not say anything that day, for he said, it is an occurrence" - to teach you that had it truly been an "occurrence" [meaning, ritual impurity from nocturnal emission], he would not have come to his own table. Ten: that he sanctified consecrated things, as it is said (I Chronicles 26:28), "and all that Samuel the seer had dedicated, and Saul son of Kish." Eleven: that he made his own honor equal to his servant's honor, as it is said (I Samuel 20:25), "and the king sat upon his seat, as at other times, upon a seat by the wall," and so on. Twelve: that he was easily appeased - you find that when David appeased him in the cave, he was immediately appeased, as it is said (I Samuel 26:21), "and Saul said, I have sinned; return, my son David." Thirteen: that he knew David was destined to reign, and sought help from him, as it is said (I Samuel 24:20), "and now, behold, I know that you shall surely reign, and the kingdom of Israel shall be established in your hand," and so on.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:45: Great is humility, through which David became great, as it is said (I Chronicles 17:16-17), "and King David came and sat before the LORD, and said, who am I," and so on, and it is written, "and You have regarded me according to the estate of a man of high degree," and so on. He said to Him, Master of the universe, what am I, that You have compared me to Jacob our father, peace be upon him, who is engraved on the Throne, in the form of man, engraved above - and so Israel ask (Jeremiah 14:21), "do not disgrace the throne of Your glory" - that very form engraved on the Throne. And from where do we know that He compared him to the Patriarchs? As it is said (II Samuel 7:9), "and I have made you a name like the name of the great ones who are on the earth." Although he had all these attributes and all this honor, and was the anointed of the God of Jacob, and the sweet singer of Israel, and praised for several attributes - "skilled in playing, a mighty man of valor, a man of war, prudent in speech," and so on (I Samuel 16:18) - and killed the lion and the bear in the field, and killed Goliath the Philistine, was the king's son-in-law, and obeyed him, and was honored in his house, and he saved Israel from the hand of the Philistines - and after all this he was lowly in his own eyes and humble, and said to Saul, when he pursued him (I Samuel 24:15), "after whom has the king of Israel come out? After whom do you pursue? After a dead dog, after one flea," and so on - and after all this honor, he reigned over Israel and Judah and conquered several kingdoms, and said (Psalms 22:7), "and I am a worm, and not a man," and so on - and when he brought up the Ark of God from the house of Oved Edom the Gittite to the City of David, he danced, and so on, as we elaborated in the last chapter of the Gate of Fear.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 7:46: Great is humility, for which Mordechai was praised - for at first he was fifth in the Sanhedrin, as it is said (Ezra 2:2), "who came with Zerubbabel, Yeshua, Nechemyah, Serayah, Re'elayah, Mordechai" - and once he became viceroy to the king, it was not enough for him that he did not wish to be fourth, but he did not even wish to be fifth in his own place - rather, although his greatness increased, he lowered himself and became sixth, as it is said (Nehemiah 7:7), "those who came with Zerubbabel, Yeshua, Nechemyah, Azaryah, Ra'amyah, Nachamani, Mordechai."
